title: Hobbies and how often
goal: Talk about what you like and how often you do it — while adding -(으)러 가요, the Korean way of saying why you're going somewhere.
bekal: naming hobbies and asking about other people's
telling 좋다 from 좋아하다, and 잘하다 from 못하다
saying how often with frequency adverbs
using -(으)러 가요 to say what you're going somewhere to do

dialogs.title: 대화 — What do you usually do on weekends?
dialogs.intro: Minjun and Ani ask each other about hobbies. Watch for the pattern -(으)러 가요, which comes up several times and fills a big gap in your storytelling.

notes: **-(으)러 가요 means "go (somewhere) to do something".** It states the **purpose** of going, and it's the only natural way to say it in Korean. 수영하**러** 가요 = go swimming (go in order to swim). Without this pattern you're stuck saying two separate sentences, which sounds stiff.
**⚠️ -(으)러 only pairs with verbs of motion:** 가다, 오다, 다니다. There's no 수영하러 좋아해요. If the main verb isn't one of motion, you use -기 위해서 (in order to), which waits for B1.

**좋다 and 좋아하다 are not the same thing, and they take different particles.** 운동**이** 좋아요 = exercise is good (an adjective, describing the thing). 운동**을** 좋아해요 = I like exercise (a verb, someone does the liking). Mixing them up is one of the most common learner mistakes.

**잘하다 and 못하다 are a pair too.** 노래를 **잘해요** = I'm good at singing. 수영을 **못해요** = I can't swim, in the sense of not being good at it. ⚠️ Note that 못해요 here is written as one word and means "be bad at", unlike 못 해요 written separately, which means "can't get it done".

**사진 찍는 거 좋아해요 uses a verb turned into a noun.** The ending -는 거 turns a verb into "the doing of": 찍는 거 = taking (photos), 먹는 거 = eating — much like English "-ing" after "like". The full form waits for B1; for now learn **[verb]는 거 좋아해요** as one template.

**-아/어 봤어요 means "have tried".** 가 봤어요 = I've been (and tried it). 먹어 봤어요 = I've tasted it. The negative is 안 가 봤어요 (I've never been). It's the most common way to ask about experience in everyday Korean.

**대단해요 means "impressive", praising someone's effort.** Together with 잘하네요 ("you're good at that") and 멋있어요 ("cool"), it's part of the stock of compliments used constantly in Korean conversation. Praising the person you're talking to is part of good manners, not empty flattery.
**기대돼요 means "I'm looking forward to it".** The closest one-word English is "can't wait". It's very common as a reaction to fun plans.

grammars.title: -(으)러 가요 — go to do
body: Attach **-러** to vowel stems, **-으러** to consonant stems, then follow with a verb of motion.
after: **The destination comes before the whole chain:** 도서관에 공부하러 가요 = go to the library to study. The order is place – purpose – verb of motion.
**This is one of the patterns that most quickly makes your Korean sound grown-up**, because beginners usually split it into two sentences: 도서관에 가요. 그리고 공부해요. Correct, but stiff.

grammars.title: How often
body: Frequency adverbs go **before the verb**, like all Korean adverbs.
after: ⚠️ **별로, 거의 and 전혀 must be followed by a negative.** 별로 좋아해요 is not a sentence; the correct form is 별로 **안** 좋아해요. Same double-negative pattern as 아무것도 in unit 7.
**별로 안 좋아해요 is the gentlest way to say you don't like something.** Saying 싫어해요 ("hate") is much stronger than most learners mean, and often startles the listener.

blocks.text: Most words in this table are nouns, and they become verbs just by adding 하다: 운동하다, 수영하다, 등산하다, 요리하다, 여행하다. Back to the lesson of unit 5 — 하다 is the verb-making machine of Korean.

head: Sentence
Meaning
rows: I go swimming three times a week.

blocks.title: 노래방 and why you can't avoid it
items: **노래방** (literally "song room") is a karaoke booth rented by the hour, and it's a fixture of Korean social life — almost every get-together ends there.
Refusing to sing causes more trouble than singing badly. Have one song you really know by heart; the quality of your voice is never the point.
⚠️ The songbook has a foreign-songs section, usually under 팝송. English songs are almost always there, along with popular songs from many other countries.
